title: Hemoglobin alpha-like subunit mu is expressed during ontogeny and is elevated in alpha thalassemia

All other rights reserved. The alpha globin gene cluster on chromosome 16 encodes alpha-like globins whose expression changes during development. HBM located in this cluster was considered a pseudogene until its transcript was discovered in 2005, but without a detectable protein product. Here, we provide the first detailed description of HBM -encoded globin at the protein level (hemoglobin mu chain [HBM]) across different age groups using liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry. Using targeted analysis, we demonstrate that HBM protein is readily detectable in circulation with its levels falling with increasing gestational age. We also report HBM levels in relation to other hemoglobin chains in neonatal, pediatric, and adult blood. Furthermore, analysis of alpha thalassemia patient samples revealed that HBM levels were elevated 3- to 17-fold, indicating a compensatory role, which could be explored for its therapeutic potential. This study enhances our understanding of erythropoiesis and globin chain production through ontogeny. pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript yes pmc-prop-open-manuscript yes pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC-ND Introduction The protein component of hemoglobin is encoded by alpha- and beta-globin gene clusters located on chromosomes 16 and 11, respectively. The alpha-globin gene cluster includes the following genes and pseudogenes (prefixed with ψ), in order: 5′ -ζ ( HBZ )-ψζ-μ ( HBM )-ψα1-α2 ( HBA2 )-α1 ( HBA1 )-θ ( HBQ1 )-3′ 1 ( Figure 1A ). Different globin subunits participate in the formation of hemoglobin through ontogeny. 2 , 3 In the embryonic stage, 3 forms are known to be produced in the yolk sac up to 9 weeks of gestation: Hb Portland-1 (globin tetramer with composition ζ2γ2), Hb Gower-1 (ζ2ε2), and Hb Gower-2 (α2ε2). 4 , 5 As erythropoiesis migrates from the yolk sac to the fetal liver, the alpha-like HBZ (ζ) chain is replaced by the fetal/adult HBA (α), which is encoded by both HBA1 and HBA2 . 6 HBM , located between the pseudogenes ψζ1 and ψα1, was also considered a pseudogene until its transcript was discovered in umbilical cord blood in 2005. 7 , 8 Based on this discovery of the RNA product, HBM was classified as a gene although its protein product, predicted to have a sequence highly homologous to the other alpha-like chains ( Figure 1B ), was not detected by mass spectrometry at the time. Alpha thalassemias are often caused by deletional pathogenic variants in HBA1 and/or HBA2 , although nondeletional variants also exist. It has been estimated that ~20% to 30% of the world’s population are carriers of such variants. 9 , 10 Deletional alpha thalassemias are classified as α + - or α 0 -thalassemia based on whether 1 or 2 alpha globin genes are deleted (or reduced in activity), respectively. Clinical presentation can vary widely in severity from resulting in stillbirth to being asymptomatic, correlating with the number of functional alpha globin genes inherited. 11 Two common forms of α + -thalassemia are −α 3.7 and −α 4.2 , where the superscript refers to the length of the genomic deletion in kilobase units. Two common forms of α 0 -thalassemias are – – Med and – – SEA , with their superscripts referring to geographic regions where they are prevalent, that is, the Mediterranean region and Southeast Asia, respectively. 9 As found in Figure 1A , the −α 3.7 deletion spares both HBM and HBZ , whereas the – – SEA form results in the loss of HBM while sparing HBZ . 12 Here, we used high-resolution targeted mass spectrometry analysis to demonstrate that the protein product of HBM is expressed not only at early fetal stages but also into late gestation. Using blood samples from premature and term newborns and pediatric and adult donors, we provide evidence for declining levels of HBM with age and low level of expression well into adulthood. Finally, we also demonstrate that HBM level is elevated in patients with deletional alpha thalassemias where it likely plays a compensatory role. Methods Samples of peripheral and umbilical cord blood were collected from adults, pediatric subjects, and neonates with consent. The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee (Mayo Clinic Institutional Review Board: 21-012890). Proteins were extracted from dried blood spots, and, in solution, digestion was performed with trypsin to generate peptides. Discovery analysis was carried out on a Thermo Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid mass spectrometer to identify globin chains. A targeted mass spectrometry analysis method using liquid chromatography–selected reaction monitoring was developed and optimized using heavy standards for each globin on a Thermo TSQ Altis triple quadrupole system. Skyline software was used for data analysis. Quantitation values for globin chains were calculated relative to the spiked-in internal standards. See the supplemental Methods for further details. Results When our group published the first draft map of the human proteome in 2014, 13 HBM was identified at the protein level for the first time in fetal tissues, including the heart, liver, gut, brain, and placenta, while remaining undetected in adult tissues ( Figure 1C ). We wondered whether this alpha-like globin chain was only expressed during development or whether it is also present at birth and thereafter. Therefore, we performed proteomics analysis of blood samples from newborns using highly sensitive liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry–based discovery methods. We included peripheral or umbilical cord blood samples from neonates born at different gestational ages ( supplemental Table 1 ). Even as the abundant chains HBA, HBB, HBD, HBG1, and HBG2 and less abundant chains HBZ, HBE, and HBQ1 were detected in all samples, to our surprise, HBM was also detected in all samples with excellent sequence coverage ( Figure 1D ; supplemental Figure 1 ). This indicates that the protein HBM is present in circulation at detectable amounts even after birth. Next, to quantify HBM levels along with all other globin subunits, we developed a targeted selected reaction monitoring assay using synthetic heavy stable isotope-labeled peptide standards 14 ( supplemental Table 2 ). We deployed this method to analyze dried blood spot samples from 29 individuals including neonates born preterm or at term, pediatric subjects up to 5 years of age, and 10 volunteer adult donors ( supplemental Tables 1 and 3 ). Interestingly, HBM protein was detected in all tested samples, including adult samples. It was detected at higher levels in preterm newborns compared with others, with its levels decreasing in neonates with increasing gestational age, continuing to do so with postnatal age ( Figure 2A ). Between 3 and 5 years of age, HBM concentration plateaued at low levels, where it remained into adulthood. Based on these observations, it seems fair to surmise that HBM is expressed in ontogeny and likely follows a pattern of expression similar to known embryonic and fetal globins. Next, we applied the targeted assay for quantifying all globin chains to investigate the relative contribution of each chain to the total globin complement in each sample. The embryonic globin subunits HBE and HBZ, along with subunit HBM, contributed under 1% of total intensity of globins. The relative contribution of these 3 subunits is found in Figure 2B . Among the neonatal blood samples, HBM constituted 0.04% to 0.08% of all globin chains. HBM levels were the highest among premature newborns, with an average of 0.07%. HBM levels fell to under an average of 0.06% of total globins in term newborns. The levels continue to decrease in pediatric (age 1-5 years) and adult subjects, averaging ~0.002% of total globins, which corresponds to a 30-fold decrease from the levels observed at birth. HBE and HBZ, which are known to form tetramers in the embryonic stage of hematopoiesis, 4 were both detected in a similar pattern in neonatal samples. Evidently, HBM has levels of expression in the late gestational period which are comparable to HBE and HBZ. These data reveal that these 3 hemoglobin chains also have similar trends of change with age, both during gestation and postnatally ( Figure 2B ). We therefore hypothesize that HBM is an embryonic alpha-like globin chain like HBZ. We wondered whether HBM levels are affected in alpha thalassemia. We tested 14 individuals with alpha thalassemia representing the following 3 molecular subtypes: heterozygous 17.5 kb deletion, that is, Southeast Asian deletion (– – SEA /αα), heterozygous 3.7 kb deletion (−α 3.7 /αα), and homozygous 3.7 kb deletion (−α 3.7 /−α 3.7 ). Using the targeted assay for hemoglobin chains, we calculated HBM levels (as well as HBZ) in these individuals along with volunteer donor adults. Interestingly, HBM levels were elevated 3- to 17-fold in individuals with the thalassemia variant with a 3.7 kb deletion in the homozygous state (−α 3.7 /−α 3.7 ), but they were only modestly increased in those with a heterozygous 3.7 kb deletion (−α 3.7 /αα) and those with the heterozygous Southeast Asian variant (– – SEA /αα) genotypes ( Figure 2C ). This may be explained by the segment that is deleted in these genotypes and the location of HBM gene with respect to the deletion ( Figure 1A ). The compensatory increase of fetal hemoglobin in cases of beta thalassemia is a well-known phenomenon. 15 Our data indicate that HBM probably has a similar compensatory role in alpha thalassemia which may correlate with genotype. This is similar to the known compensatory role of HBZ in alpha thalassemias, which we also observed ( Figure 2D ). In the Southeast Asian variant (– – SEA /αα) where a large section of the alpha gene locus is deleted in the heterozygous state, HBZ , which is spared from deletion, is expressed at higher levels than HBM , which is within the deleted portion. However, in 3.7 kb deletional alpha thalassemia where both HBM and HBZ are spared, their protein products are both elevated ( Figure 1A ). Our observations corroborate reports by others who note elevation of HBM and HBZ levels in various alpha thalassemia subtypes 16 and suggest that these globins could be potential markers for alpha thalassemia screening. Discussion Taken together, our data reveal that the HBM gene encodes a protein product expressed in adults at low levels. Higher HBM levels in the fetus are indicative of a role in ontogeny which is likely taken over by other globin chains after birth. The pattern of expression of HBM indicates that it is likely another embryonic globin chain like HBE and HBZ, which is incorporated in a similar fashion into hemoglobin tetramers during early development. However, because our study did not include embryonic/fetal tissue samples from different stages of development, a detailed investigation is needed to discern its temporal expression during fetal stages of development. Our data also reveal that HBM is a candidate biomarker that could be used for screening of some cases of alpha thalassemia, and this potential could be tested in larger cohorts. Additional studies will be necessary to fully understand the mechanisms of any compensation such as gene competition and autonomous silencing. 17 Such studies may also shed light on the biochemical properties of HBM protein, such as stability and oxygen dissociation, and facilitate development of novel therapies for alpha thalassemias where the HBM gene is spared. Supplementary Material 1 Key Points Hemoglobin subunit mu (HBM) is an alpha-like globin chain that is expressed during gestation at levels similar to embryonic globins. HBM levels are elevated in some patients with alpha thalassemia likely because of compensation and could serve as a diagnostic biomarker.
